title: America Turns 250 Tomorrow. No Immigrant Community Has Risen Faster Than Indian Americans.
excerpt: As the U.S. marks its semiquincentennial, 5.2 million Indian Americans — now the country's largest Asian ethnic group — are reshaping everything from the C-suite to Capitol Hill. Their story is also getting more complicated.
body:
As the United States prepares to celebrate the 250th anniversary of its founding on July 4, the Indian American community finds itself in a paradoxical position: more visible, more powerful, and more scrutinised than at any point in its history.

The numbers tell one story. There are now more than 5.2 million people of Indian origin in the United States, making them the largest Asian ethnic group in the country. They surpassed Chinese Americans for that distinction in the 2020 census and have only widened the gap since. Between 2010 and 2020, the Indian American population grew by nearly 55 per cent. Indians are now the second-largest foreign-born immigrant group in the country, after Mexicans.

## A Disproportionate Footprint

The community's economic influence dwarfs its demographic size. According to a report by Indiaspora and Boston Consulting Group, Indian Americans pay roughly 5 to 6 per cent of all income taxes in the United States despite making up just 1.5 per cent of the population — approximately $250 to $300 billion annually.

Sixteen Indian-origin chief executives now head Fortune 500 companies, including Microsoft's Satya Nadella, Google's Sundar Pichai, and Vertex Pharmaceuticals' Reshma Kewalramani. These leaders collectively employ 2.7 million Americans and generate close to $1 trillion in revenue. The median household income for Indian Americans stands at $120,000, nearly double the national figure of $62,000.

In research and innovation, the trajectory is similarly outsized. Between 1975 and 2019, the share of U.S. patents with Indian-origin innovators jumped from around 2 per cent to 10 per cent. In recent years, research groups with scientists of Indian origin have claimed about 11 per cent of all National Institutes of Health grants and contributed to 13 per cent of scientific publications.

## The Celebration of Two Democracies

The 250th anniversary has become an occasion for the diaspora to publicly mark its dual identity. In New Jersey, the Asian American Republican Coalition and Hillsborough Maharaja Club hosted a vibrant July 4 gathering, with Mayor John Ciccarelli and Deputy Mayor Catherine Payne joining Indian American community leaders. "This gathering is not just a celebration of our nation's independence," said AARC founder Hemant Bhatt. "It's a reflection of how Asian American communities are committed to contributing meaningfully to the fabric of this great country."

In India, the U.S. Embassy has been marking the milestone with reciprocal warmth. Ambassador Sergio Gor led celebrations in both Hyderabad and Chennai, calling the events "a testament to the strong friendship and enduring partnership between the United States and India." Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay attended the Chennai reception, reflecting the deepening state-level engagement.

"That dynamic relationship between our two leaders and that trust that exists unlock an unlimited potential," Gor said, referring to the rapport between President Trump and Prime Minister Modi. "I truly believe that these few years will impact the next few decades of the world."

## Rising Prominence, Rising Tensions

But the community's ascent has not been frictionless. The Carnegie Endowment's 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey, a nationally representative poll of 1,000 Indian American adults conducted between November 2025 and January 2026, found the community navigating what it called "a convergence of cross-pressures."

On one hand, the 2024 presidential election saw a meaningful increase in Indian American support for Donald Trump, weakening — though not overturning — the community's long-standing embrace of the Democratic Party. On the other, commentators have observed a notable rise in online hate speech and discrimination targeting Indian Americans.

The survey noted that these developments "sharpen the challenge of understanding how Indian Americans are navigating electoral politics, policy change, and debates over identity and belonging in the United States, at a moment of unusual political flux."

Roughly 150 Indian Americans hold notable positions in the federal administration. The community has also produced some of the most prominent figures in the current political landscape, from former Vice President Kamala Harris to Vivek Ramaswamy, Usha Vance, and Kash Patel — spanning the ideological spectrum.

## What Comes Next

As fireworks light up American skies this July Fourth, the Indian diaspora will be watching from both sides of the Pacific. In the United States, community organisations from New Jersey to the Pacific Northwest are hosting celebrations that blend star-spangled patriotism with samosas and Bollywood. In India, U.S. consulates in Hyderabad, Chennai, and beyond have turned the 250th anniversary into a celebration of bilateral ties.

The next 250 years of the American experiment will be shaped, in no small part, by the community that arrived in force only in the last few decades. Whether it is the engineers building the AI systems that power Silicon Valley, the doctors staffing rural hospitals across the Midwest, or the entrepreneurs creating jobs in every state, Indian Americans have staked a claim on the American story that the country's founders could never have imagined.

The question is no longer whether Indian Americans belong. It is how they choose to wield the influence they have built — and whether the country they have adopted will continue to welcome them as it has.
